title: Magic-state factories under demand
summary: A magic-state factory keeps only some of its attempts (postselection), so its output time is random. How many factories a stream of T gates needs, what a single factory latency misses, and who starves when requests have priorities.
method: The two factories reproduced on digital twins on this site: magic state cultivation on the Willow twin (an attempt takes 7.24 µs, 62.8% kept) and 5-to-1 distillation on the Gemini twin (1.63 ms, 5.2% kept). A request holds a factory until an attempt is kept. Requests arrive at a fixed interval and queue on F factories.

sections.heading: Factories needed, and what a single latency gives
Priorities near saturation (4 factories, 20% urgent requests)

findings: Declaring one attempt as the factory's latency never keeps up. Declaring the mean keeps up only at low demand. Declaring the 99th percentile keeps up but needs 2 to 4 times the factories a queue needs.
Strict priority protects urgent T gates and starves background requests as the load approaches 1.

In the runs above the runtime's schedule of T injection misses its windows by 4 ns: a factory's one-qubit gates follow a reset on the same qubits with no gap, and the hardware starts them a little later. The runtime simulator does not model that turnaround.

note: All numbers are measured on QuantumOS's Lean model of RISC-Q control hardware (its cores, hubs and lanes are checked against RISC-Q's RTL cycle for cycle), on generated or published hardware designs. They are properties of that model, not of laboratory hardware.
